clue.text: Maiden intends stirring within, not yet up, preoccupied

indicators.note: within tells us the mixed letters sit inside the phrase that follows

parts.note: still in bed, not yet risen

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters of the maiden and the word after it get rearranged

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman still lying in bed, plans swirling in her head, is lost in thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' is the cricket term for an over with no runs scored, abbreviated M; it is not a young woman here.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone absent-minded is distracted and lost in thought, which is what preoccupied means.

clue.text: Aussie balls being bowled on short slope, English lost

indicators.note: short means cut down, so the word loses its end
lost signals that the letter for English is dropped

parts.note: b is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
o is a short form of on
a rake is a slope, as of a stage

explanation.surface: Cricket balls are sent down on a short sloping pitch after the English side has lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' means nonsense, not cricket balls. RAKE losing its E covers both 'short' and 'English lost'.
explanation.definitionFit: Borak is Australian slang for nonsense or banter, and balls is British slang for nonsense too.

clue.text: Grub dropping off fir trees — it causes severe itching

indicators.note: dropping off means the word's own 'off' letters fall away

parts.note: scoff is slang for food
Abies is the botanical genus of firs

explanation.surface: A larva falls from conifers, and its bite leaves a terrible itch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' looks like a larva but means food, SCOFF; the OFF inside it is what drops off.
explanation.definitionFit: Scabies is a skin disease caused by burrowing mites, marked by intense itching.

clue.text: Mild old-fashioned oath, as nothing in convent?

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

parts.note: the women living in a convent are nuns
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A gentle curse of the kind never heard in a convent.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes after the first letter of NUNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Nouns is an archaic minced oath, a softened form of 'wounds' as in 'God's wounds'.

clue.text: Run off for a moment? It's thrilling

indicators.note: off means removed, so the run word is taken away from the front

parts.note: fleetingly means briefly, for a moment
to flee is to run away, removed here

explanation.surface: Dashing off for a brief moment is exciting.
explanation.walkthrough: FLEE comes off the front of FLEETINGLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tingly causes a prickling sensation of excitement, so it is thrilling.

clue.text: Male accompanying 'pure' woman, attractive old thing

parts.note: M is short for male
Agnes is a name traditionally taken to mean pure or chaste

explanation.surface: A man escorts a chaste woman, who finds him a charming old fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attractive' means magnetic, not good-looking: magnes is an old word for the magnet or lodestone.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnes is an archaic term for a magnet or lodestone, an object that literally attracts.

clue.text: I end up under rain, shivering — would-be scary 'business'

indicators.note: shivering means shaking, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: Someone ends up standing in the rain, trembling, after a would-be fright.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'under' puts the second piece below the first. Niramiai is the sumo ritual of glaring at an opponent before a bout.
explanation.definitionFit: Niramiai is the sumo stare-down meant to intimidate, so it is an attempt at scaring the opponent.

clue.text: D = dead (late, otherwise)

parts.note: d is short for dead, as in genealogies

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style gloss: D stands for dead, also put as late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' looks like a synonym for dead in the gloss, but it is the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Delta is the code word for D in the NATO phonetic alphabet, and the Greek letter equivalent to D.

clue.text: Some reinvent it, learning style

indicators.note: some means only part of what follows, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: Some people reinvent a subject by finding their own way of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: To entitle someone is to give them a name or title, which is what to style means.

clue.text: DJ cut short disc, making Scots cheerful

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter of the word is lopped off

parts.note: a DJ is a disc jockey, colloquially a jock
a disc is round, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A disc jockey's set ends early, and the record still leaves a Scottish crowd happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Joco is a Scots word meaning jovial or pleased with oneself, a dialect synonym for cheerful.

clue.text: A round object in black stone, Chinese, showing blend of styles

indicators.note: in places the first pieces within the stone

parts.note: jet is a black stone used in jewellery
taken as written
a cob is a rounded lump, such as a cob loaf
the Han are China's main ethnic group

explanation.surface: A round thing set in jet, made in China, mixes several designs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinese' looks like a description of the stone but supplies the dynasty and people name.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacobethan describes architecture combining Jacobean and Elizabethan features, so it is a blend of two styles.

clue.text: Shakespearean character (when getting look in)

indicators.note: getting here means receiving something inside, so one word takes the other in

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he left'
mien is a person's look or bearing

explanation.surface: A note that a stage character appears when someone glances in.
explanation.walkthrough: Amiens is a lord attending the banished Duke in As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiens is a named role in As You Like It, so he is a character from Shakespeare's plays.

clue.text: Material for making tools — hassle with tree chopping

indicators.note: chopping cuts things up, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cutting down a tree is a hassle that needs the right tools.
explanation.definitionFit: Shear steel is a high-quality blister steel traditionally used for making cutting tools.

clue.text: Bellbird, far from loud, seen in tangled guaraná

indicators.note: tangled means knotted out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical marking for soft
taken as written, accent dropped

explanation.surface: A quiet bird is spotted in a thicket of guaraná, a South American climbing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The soft P joins the plant's letters before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The arapunga is a South American bird named for its loud bell-like call, so it is a kind of bellbird.

clue.text: Murderer accepts reduced breadth, shut in confined space

indicators.note: accepts means taking something in, so the murderer's name holds the next piece

parts.note: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis
breadth reduced to its abbreviation B

explanation.surface: A killer, short of room, is locked into a cramped cell.
explanation.walkthrough: B goes inside CAIN. The answer is a verb here: to cabin is to confine, as in Macbeth's 'cabin'd, cribb'd, confin'd'.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to cabin means to enclose someone in a cramped place, the sense used in Macbeth.

clue.text: Jacques (say) having little English, chat's a poor one

parts.note: Jacques Tati, the French comic film-maker, is one example of a Jacques
E is the short form of English

explanation.surface: A Frenchman with little English finds his attempts at small talk come out poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chat' is not conversation but a small, inferior potato; tatie is a dialect word for potato, listed in Chambers under tater.
explanation.definitionFit: A chat is an undersized potato, so it is a poor specimen of a tatie, a dialect word for potato.

clue.text: Sickening talent — active exercise limited

indicators.note: limited means bounded, so the talent word encloses the exercise words

parts.note: nous is common sense or know-how
a is the grammatical abbreviation for active
to exercise a right is to use it

explanation.surface: A gifted athlete's exercise routine is curtailed, which is gutting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talent' here is practical good sense, not artistic gift.
explanation.definitionFit: Nauseous means causing nausea, so it describes something sickening.

clue.text: Meal spilt round rug causing arguments

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the mixed letters wrap the floor covering
something spilt is scattered, so the letters of the meal are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a mat is a small rug

explanation.surface: Food dropped on the carpet starts a family row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arguments' are logical premises, not quarrels.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemmata is the plural of lemma, a premise or proposition assumed in an argument, so it can stand for arguments.

clue.text: Once desolate through inhaling crack

indicators.note: inhaling means drawing something in, so one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: by means through, as in 'by means of'
a leak is a crack or hole that lets something through

explanation.surface: Someone left forlorn after breathing in a hard drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like the drug but is a split or leak. 'Once' marks the answer as an obsolete word.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleaky is an old variant of bleak, meaning bare and dreary, so it matches desolate.

clue.text: Gulls left dry before river rises

parts.note: L is short for left
arid means dry

indicators.note: in a down clue, rises means read upwards, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: the Ea is a river in Chambers' list of short rivers; ea is also an old word for river

explanation.surface: Seabirds have left a dried-up spot before the river floods.
explanation.definitionFit: Laridae is the zoological family name of gulls and terns.

clue.text: Ismailian, he: 'I am involved with — line' maybe?

definitions.text: Ismailian, he: 'I am involved with — line' maybe?

indicators.note: involved means tangled together, so the letters are jumbled
the dash marks a blank, so the following words are taken out of the earlier letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, to be removed
taken as written, to be removed

explanation.surface: An Ismaili explains which branch of Islam he follows, leaving a blank for its name.
explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: the letters of 'Ismailian, he' equal those of I AM, LINE and the answer together, so removing the first two leaves the answer's letters. The whole clue is the definition: Ismailis are a Shia branch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ismailis are a branch of Shia Islam, so an Ismaili would name Shia as the line he belongs to.

clue.text: Bare patches more fitting on diner's fish served up?

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means brought upwards, so the letters read in reverse

parts.note: apter is the comparative of apt
ai, Chambers' variant of the fish ide, eaten by diners

explanation.surface: More suitable bare plates on which to serve a diner's fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in a down clue puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Apteria are the bare areas of a bird's skin between the feather tracts, so they are bare patches.

clue.text: Calamari queen rejected for pork

definitions.note: pork here in its obsolete sense of a pig

indicators.note: rejected means thrown out, so the queen's letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: calamari is squid served as food
Q is the abbreviation for queen, as in chess

explanation.surface: A queen refuses the squid dish and orders pork instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Pork is an old word for a pig, and a suid is any member of the pig family.
explanation.definitionFit: A suid is an animal of the pig family Suidae, and pork once meant a pig itself.

clue.text: Empty heads of last in class, dense — what's to be done about that?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the deed word goes around the chosen letters

parts.note: a deed is something done

indicators.note: last in picks out the final letter of each of the next words

parts.note: the end of the word
the end of the word

explanation.surface: A teacher wonders what to do about empty-headed pupils, the bottom of the class and dense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads' tempts the solver to take first letters, but it belongs to the definition: seed heads emptied. The last letters of class and dense go inside DEED.
explanation.definitionFit: To deseed is to remove the seeds from something, such as a seed head of a plant, emptying it.

clue.text: Ship rounding headland makes getaway

indicators.note: rounding means going around, so the ship's letters surround the headland

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
a cape is a headland

explanation.surface: A vessel slips round a promontory to escape pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: Scape is an archaic form of escape.
explanation.definitionFit: Scape is an old shortened form of escape, so scapes means escapes or makes a getaway.

clue.text: Coy old maidens, covering head, in a tizzy

indicators.note: in a tizzy means flustered, so the letters are thrown into disorder
covering the head hides it, so the first letter disappears

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Bashful girls of yesteryear hide their faces in a fluster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coy' is the Shakespearean verb meaning disdain, not the adjective shy; 'old' signals archaic. Sdaine is Spenser's form of disdain.
explanation.definitionFit: Sdaine is Spenserian for disdain, and to coy is an obsolete verb meaning to disdain.

clue.text: Heart's given out — died, worn out

indicators.note: given out suggests something broken down, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A cardiac failure leads to death through exhaustion.
explanation.definitionFit: Trashed is slang for exhausted or ruined, so it fits worn out.

clue.text: Is it seen in Imari tableware? Yes and no (strictly speaking)

definitions.text: Is it seen in Imari tableware? Yes and no (strictly speaking)

indicators.note: seen in means the letters can be spotted inside the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A collector asks whether a famous Japanese porcelain is part of Imari ware.
explanation.walkthrough: Imari ware is porcelain made at Arita and shipped from the port of Imari, so the name is both in it and, strictly, not.
explanation.definitionFit: Arita is the Japanese porcelain town whose wares were exported through Imari, so Imari ware is Arita ware under another name.

clue.text: No place for a captured ranker or aged gaolbird

definitions.text: No place for a captured ranker

parts.note: of can mean aged, as in 'a man of sixty'
a lag is a convict

explanation.surface: Prison is no place for a common soldier or an old convict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aged gaolbird' suggests old lag, but aged gives OF. An Oflag was a German prison camp for captured officers, so not for ordinary rankers.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oflag held officer prisoners of war, so it was not where a captured private or other ranker was sent.

clue.text: Fawn mushroom, almost scarlet inside?

indicators.note: inside places the shortened colour within the mushroom

parts.note: a cep is an edible mushroom, the porcino

parts.note: scarlet is a shade of red

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fawn' looks like a colour but is the verb, to grovel.
explanation.definitionFit: To fawn is to flatter obsequiously, and to creep is to behave in the same servile way.

clue.text: Displaying crisp image, is engaging

definitions.meaning: second meaning: employs someone, takes on for pay

explanation.surface: A sharp picture on screen is attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as hi-res for the first meaning, and as one word, a verb, for the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Hi-res describes a high-resolution display, and hires means takes on staff, just as engaging does.

clue.text: Like a proud 'dame' and one-time spouse

definitions.meaning: first meaning: French for proud, feminine form, as a dame would be described
second meaning: an obsolete word for a companion or spouse, a variant of fere

explanation.surface: A haughty lady and her former husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dame' in quotes points to French, where the adjective takes a feminine ending. 'One-time' marks the second meaning as archaic, not as an ex.
explanation.definitionFit: French fière is the feminine of proud, and fiere is an old Scots and English spelling of fere, a mate or spouse.

clue.text: Aunt shocked about nakedness

explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal but here supplies RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nature can mean the unclothed state, as in being in a state of nature, that is, stark naked.

clue.text: Line that is penned by form in school ass omitted

omitted means left out, so those letters are removed from the word

parts.note: a form in school is a class
taken as written, to be removed
i.e. is short for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A school line where a donkey has been left out of the class list.
explanation.walkthrough: CLASS loses ASS to give CL, which then pens IE. Ciel is a variant of ceil, to line a ceiling or wall.
explanation.definitionFit: To ciel or ceil is to cover an inner surface such as a ceiling with panelling, so it means to line.

parts.note: taken as written
